To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the number of hot pixel defects in image sensors increases over time in a way that can be predicted by an empirical formula that depends on the pixel size, sensor size, and gain (ISO).
the defect density is proportional to sensor area and that the defect density for CCD imagers scales to the pixel size with an exponent -2.25 and for APS imagers with an exponent -3.07.

the defect densities of CCD imagers are proportional to the square of the pixel size and to the ISO to the 0.69 power, and that for APS sensors the defect densities are inversely proportional to the cube of the pixel size, and to the ISO raised to 0.5 power.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model for the defect density of image sensors, based on pixel size and ISO. Proc. SPIE 6069, Sensors and Camera Systems for
the development of an analytical model that predicts the rate of permanent hot pixel defects in digital cameras as a function of sensor area, pixel size, and ISO setting.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the defect density for CCD sensors is proportional to pixel size to the -2.25 power times the ISO to 0.69 power, while for CMOS sensors the power law is proportional to pixel to the -3.07 power times the ISO 0.5 power.

the defect density for CCD and CMOS sensors scales with pixel size and ISO according to the following power laws: CCD: defect density = 1.2e-6*pixel size^(-2.25)*ISO^0.69 APS (CMOS): defect density = 2.3e-7*pixel size^3.07*ISO^0.5 The power law fits are shown to be accurate for the range of parameters used in our tests.
hot pixel defects are a function of the pixel size, sensor size and gain (ISO) and that this function is well represented by a power law.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the defect density for hot pixel defects in image sensors is a function of the pixel size and the ISO, and it is independent of the technology.
the rate of permanent hot pixel defects in image sensors is a function of the sensor size, pixel size and ISO, and the technology.
defect densities scale linearly with the area of the imager, and that the defect rate per unit area scales as the pixel size to a negative power times the ISO to a positive power.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hot pixel defect density scales linearly with sensor size and that it depends on pixel size and ISO, but not on the number of pixels.
hot pixel defects are an intrinsic part of image sensors and are a major factor in determining the lifetime of the camera.
defect rates are not only a function of pixel size but also a strong function of ISO, and therefore, a strong function of the sensor technology.
